content.text: This recipe makes 8 onigiri and takes about 20 minutes once the rice is cooked.
are Japan's answer to the packed lunch. They are shaped by hand, tucked with a flavourful filling, and wrapped in a strip of
or tuna mixed with Japanese mayonnaise. Both work in this recipe, either separately or alternating.

The rice must be warm, not hot and not cold. Rice that is too hot will burn your hands and become difficult to shape. Rice that has cooled completely will not stick together at all. Aim for the temperature of a warm bath. Keep a bowl of water with a pinch of salt beside you for wetting your hands between each ball. This stops the rice sticking to your palms.

items.prepNote: each cut in half to make 8 strips
stones removed, for half the onigiri
optional, to press onto the outside

content.text: Cook the rice according to the packet instructions. Spread it into a wide bowl and leave to cool to a warm, handleable temperature, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Mix the tuna and Japanese mayonnaise together in a small bowl. Season with a little soy sauce if you like. Set aside.
Cut each nori sheet in half. You need 8 strips total.
Prepare a bowl of cold salted water for wetting your hands. Dip your hands in the water, shake off the excess, then scoop about 80g of rice into your palm. Flatten it slightly.
Place a teaspoon of filling in the centre of the rice. For tuna-mayo, use about 15g. For umeboshi, use half a pickled plum.

Cup your hands and press the rice firmly around the filling to enclose it. Shape into a triangle by pressing with your dominant hand while cupping with your other. Press firmly and evenly three times, rotating the rice ball between each press. The triangle should hold its shape without crumbling.

Wrap a strip of nori around the base of each onigiri. If adding sesame seeds, press them gently onto the top surface. Repeat for all 8. Serve within an hour or wrap individually in cling film for a lunchbox.

items.cause: Rice was too cold or not pressed firmly enough
items.fix: Use warm rice and press much more firmly than feels comfortable. Onigiri need real compression to hold their shape.

items.symptom: The nori has gone soft and chewy
items.cause: Nori was wrapped too far in advance and absorbed moisture from the rice
items.fix: For packed lunches, wrap the nori separately and attach it just before eating. Some convenience stores use a special wrapper for exactly this reason.

items.symptom: The filling spills out when pressing
items.fix: Keep fillings to a teaspoon or 15g. Press the rice over the filling from all sides before shaping the triangle.

content.text: Onigiri have been eaten in Japan for over a thousand years. Records show warriors carrying rice balls as field rations in the Sengoku period. Today they are the best-selling item in Japanese convenience stores. Over two billion are sold every year in Japan alone. The triangle shape is a modern convenience-store standard. At home and in older regions, onigiri can be round or cylindrical. Fillings vary by region and season, but umeboshi and tuna-mayo remain the two most popular across the country.
